candidates.title: Keep received images with customer messages

demandEvidence.chore: Join a customer message with its already received image so a reply assistant does not request the image again.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: I want the AI agent to recognize that the image has already been received and use the available image to identify the product

experimentPlan.output: A review card pairing one message with its supplied image reference and a draft product question.
inputs: operator-supplied image reference or mock image description
experimentPlan.trigger: When an operator submits one fictional or consented message and its associated image reference.
steps: Store the message and image reference under one test case.
Check that both fields are present before drafting.
Prepare a short product-identification question from the supplied inputs.
Show the draft and inputs together for review.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: On a small labeled fixture set, confirm each card keeps the correct message paired with its image reference and never claims an unsupported product identity.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: A person supplies authorized inputs, verifies image interpretation and approves any customer reply.
unverified: Make execution and Messenger connector behavior
Image transfer and model image interpretation
Identification accuracy on real product images

ease.reason: A paired-input mock is manageable, but no supplied implementation reference documents Make routing or image forwarding.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: small businesses handling product inquiries might pay to reduce repeated image requests; this post shows no buying intent.

feasibility.reason: A four-week fixture test is bounded; live Messenger access, image handling and identification quality remain unverified.

autonomy.reason: A proposed draft can package supplied context, but a person must verify the image and product before replying.

evidence.reason: The retained post span describes the text and image routes and the resend problem; recurrence and implementation support are not established.

candidates.reason: Scored a bounded proposed experiment from the assigned chore; provisional mean 4.6 is below 6 and it remains rejected.

candidates.title: Explain gaps between ad and store purchase totals

demandEvidence.chore: Compare daily ad-attributed purchases with Shopify online-store orders and flag dates needing a human explanation.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: In Shopify, export daily orders for the same 30 days, Online Store channel only, without test and cancelled orders.

experimentPlan.output: A date-by-date comparison sheet that flags mismatches and offers a cautious explanation checklist.
inputs: fictional daily ad-purchase rows with attribution setting
experimentPlan.trigger: When an operator supplies two matching 30-day sample exports.
steps: Check that both tables cover the same dates.
Apply the chosen channel and exclusion labels supplied by the operator.
Compare daily totals by date.
Flag gaps without assigning a cause.
Show a checklist of possible explanations for human review.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: On hand-labeled synthetic tables, verify date alignment, exclusions and arithmetic; confirm the report never states a cause from totals alone.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: A person supplies authorized exports, confirms settings and investigates tracking or attribution before taking action.
unverified: Exact export formats and column mapping
Whether any flagged gap represents duplicate tracking

ease.reason: A beginner can compare two labeled tables, but no supplied reference supports advertising export parsing or attribution logic.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: small ecommerce operators may pay for clearer discrepancy review; this post describes a check, not buyer intent.

feasibility.reason: A four-week synthetic-table report is bounded, while live exports and correct attribution interpretation remain unverified.

autonomy.reason: A repeatable date comparison can flag differences, but a person must interpret causes and make any tracking changes.

evidence.reason: The retained task and context spans specify two exports and possible causes, but do not provide corroboration or a verified service.

candidates.reason: Scored a bounded proposed experiment from the assigned chore; provisional mean 4.8 is below 6 and it remains rejected.

candidates.title: Review possible repeats after missed schedule runs

demandEvidence.chore: Review a rerun batch for likely duplicate records before an operator resumes processing.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: Missed schedule triggers can duplicate everything.

experimentPlan.output: A review list of exact and possible duplicate rows in a supplied rerun batch.
experimentPlan.trigger: When an operator submits a suspected rerun for review.
steps: Compare rows on the supplied key.
Separate exact matches from rows with missing keys.
Flag possible repeats without deleting or skipping anything.
Show matched row references for human review.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: A labeled synthetic fixture should correctly flag exact duplicate keys and leave ambiguous or missing-key cases unresolved.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: A person selects the key, confirms each match and authorizes any skip, replay or data change.
unverified: Which record fields define a duplicate
How the scheduler recovers missed runs
Whether a flagged row is safe to skip

ease.reason: A synthetic duplicate review is approachable, but no supplied reference documents scheduler recovery or idempotency.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: workflow consultants may pay to reduce duplicate processing; this post proves no purchase intent or payment.

feasibility.reason: A four-week mock can compare fictional batch keys, while real recovery rules and identifiers are unknown.

autonomy.reason: A proposed checker can flag matching keys, but an operator must confirm matches and decide whether to resume.

evidence.reason: One retained task span identifies duplicate processing after missed triggers; frequency, fields and recovery rules are missing from these spans.

candidates.reason: Scored a bounded proposed experiment from the assigned chore; provisional mean 4.6 is below 6 and it remains rejected.

candidates.title: Review salon booking requests against test slots

demandEvidence.chore: Check a proposed salon booking request against supplied working-hour, staff-availability and existing-appointment test data.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: Atomic Slot Validation: Every booking request checks salon working hours, master availability, and existing appointments in PostgreSQL at the SQL level before confirmation.

experimentPlan.output: A proposed conflict report for fictional booking requests and salon slots.
experimentPlan.trigger: When an operator submits a sample booking request for review.
steps: Check whether the requested time falls in supplied working hours.
Compare it with supplied staff availability.
Compare it with fictional existing appointments.
Return conflict, no conflict or insufficient data.
Ask a person to review the result before confirmation.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: On labeled synthetic cases, verify known overlaps are flagged and missing availability produces an unresolved result rather than a booking confirmation.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: A person supplies and validates the test rules and authorizes all real bookings; the prototype does not reserve or persist slots.
unverified: Whether the showcased architecture works outside its author report

ease.reason: The post describes SQL slot checks, but no separate supplied building reference supports a beginner implementation.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: independent salons may pay to reduce booking conflicts; this maker architecture post proves no buyer intent.

feasibility.reason: A four-week synthetic slot review is bounded, while live calendar access and concurrent booking safety remain unverified.

autonomy.reason: A test checker could flag conflicts, but a person must validate availability and confirm every real booking.

evidence.reason: Retained spans describe a maker-reported booking architecture and checks; external use and independent demand are not established.

candidates.title: Prepare a review card for automation failures

demandEvidence.chore: Review an operator-reported automation failure and prepare a concise diagnostic card, with duplicate records as one possible issue.

experimentPlan.output: A review card summarizing an operator-supplied failure and listing safe next checks.
experimentPlan.trigger: When an operator submits a single failed automation example.
steps: Capture expected and observed outcomes.
Attach the supplied error text and integration label.
Show a short summary and checklist of missing information.
Route module errors to a configured Make error handler only in a separate operator-managed test.
Return the card for human diagnosis.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: For labeled synthetic cases, confirm each card preserves the supplied facts and does not invent a root cause or corrective action.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: A person supplies authorized, redacted information, diagnoses the failure and approves scenario changes; the Make documentation only describes an error route.
unverified: Whether any listed issue recurs in a specific workflow
The supplied reference does not document matching duplicates
Live execution, integration-specific causes and repairs

ease.reason: The supplied Make documentation (428eda549e557f199c3af452) supports routing module errors to a handler, not deduplication or diagnosis.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: small automation service firms may pay for organized fault review; the offer reports no completed paid work.

feasibility.reason: A four-week synthetic error-card prototype is bounded, while the listed integrations and actual causes remain unverified.

autonomy.reason: An error can be organized for review, but a person must diagnose the cause and authorize any scenario edit.

evidence.reason: The post lists duplicate records among example problems and offers fixed-price help, but no particular incident or recurrence is established.

steps.message: Assessed all ten sealed discussion assignments. Five broad or underspecified posts lack a concrete chore in supplied text; five concrete chores received bounded plans and all five provisional ratings. None meets the threshold, so no post is proposed.
